h: פָּרָשַׁת שְׁקָלִים, מַאֲמָר ה׳ Parshas Shekalim — Maamar Hei

p: "The light of Your countenance upon us,
we say this in the Mussaf prayer,
in the piyut, in every blessing.
Since the piyutim have been accepted
it is fitting to understand their words;
and even if their author and arranger
as written in Sefer Urim V'Tumim
(Kitzur Tokfo Kohen, os 123–124, at the end),
that the words of the Shulchan Aruch and the like,
which have been accepted throughout Klal Yisrael,
may fittingly be interpreted in their words
even though they did not intend this,
for the spirit of Hashem spoke through them.
for of the meal of Atika we say
is the revelation of the Forehead of Atika,
as they said in the Idra
this is the forehead and the nose."
This is "the light of Your countenance" —
the light of Atika upon us,
which is above, like a crown upon the head.
the intellect hidden from all thought;
for so the term "high and exalted" indicates
the grasp of all created beings,
The verses of the piyut begin
with the pasuk "A cluster of henna, etc."
וְהוּא עַל פִּי הַגְּמָרָא (שָׁם פח, ב)
מְכַפֵּר לִי עַל עֲווֹן גְּדִי וְכוּלֵּי
atones for me for the sin of the kid, etc." —
that is, the sin of the Golden Calf.
And the shekalim came to atone
for the sin of the Calf,
as they said in the Yerushalmi
[שְׁקָלִים פֶּרֶק ב׳ הֲלָכָה ג׳ ט, ב]
let them give half a shekel;
since they sinned at the sixth hour,
and since they transgressed the Ten Commandments,
let each one give ten gerah,"
So too it is brought in the Tanchuma (there, 2):
to Hashem Yisbarach by the title "Eshkol,"
הוּא עַל פִּי מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת יא, ב)
is based on what they said (Berachos 11b):
וַיַּרְא אֱלֹהִים אֶת כָּל אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה
"And God saw all that He had made,
and behold it was very good,"
as referring to all that is the opposite of good;
in resolving the question of the Rebbe, Rabbi Ber,
may the memory of the righteous and holy be a blessing
where is the creation of evil mentioned
And we said, based on the Gemara
and this is what is said, "and creates evil" —
"that it was good" is not said,
which alludes to the Angel of Death
שֶׁהוּא הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע [בָּבָא בַּתְרָא טז, א],
who is the yetzer hara (Bava Basra 16a),
which alludes to the deeds of the wicked,
for "that it was good" is not said of it.
So too the fire of Gehinnom,
which was created on the second day,
וְלֹא נֶאֱמַר כִּי טוֹב [פְּסָחִים נד, א].
and "that it was good" is not said (Pesachim 54a).
And afterwards, on the sixth day,
לֹא נֶאֱמַר בּוֹ גַּם כֵּן כִּי טוֹב
"that it was good" is likewise not said of him;
that is, he was created with free choice,
so that the serpent could enter him and seduce him.
וַיַּרְא אֱלֹהִים אֶת כָּל אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה
"And God saw all that He had made,
and behold it was very good":
for at the onset of Shabbos
His world found favor in His eyes,
so that from it there would come "very good";
so that there be the advantage of light over darkness,
in the manner stated in the holy Zohar
and there is no good except that
עַל מַלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת וְיֵצֶר הָרָע וְגֵיהִנֹּם
as the Angel of Death, the yetzer hara and Gehinnom,
which are called by the name "kol";
and this is why the Men of the Great Assembly euphemized
And this is "He to Whom everything belongs":
which denotes the opposite of good,
He atones for the sin of the kid
that I heaped up for myself.
And in the manner stated in the Gemara
"If your sins be like these years,
which come in their order, etc.,
they shall be made white as snow" —
so that everything will become like merits
And when the sin of the Calf is rectified
the crowns will be returned to Yisrael
that were tied on Yisrael at Mattan Torah;
and this is "the light of Your countenance upon us,
which is a crown upon the head,
from the rays of light and splendor.
that the reading of the parshah, and the yearning
to fulfill the mitzvah of shekalim,
in a House established and exalted" —
is called the Holy of Holies,
as it says in the holy Zohar
We say "And a shekel I will bring"
because the yearning is like the deed,
as we say in the Mussaf prayers,
"We will prepare and offer with love
according to the commandment of Your will."
cannot be offered on its day —
for even though on Shabbos and Yom Tov
יוּכַל בִּנְיַן הֶעָתִיד גַּם כֵּן לְהִגָּלוֹת
the future building could also be revealed,
since it is by the hands of Heaven,
(רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה ל, א דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל לֹא),
offer this Mussaf on that same day —
of "We will prepare and offer with love"
is through the yearning to do it,
since he was prevented and did not do it.
This is why we say "the commandment of Your will"
and not "the commandment of Your Torah,"
for His will, may He be blessed,
for the sake of giving satisfaction
And this is the yearning and the love
and the Holy One, blessed be He,
wants nothing from us but the heart,
as it says in the holy Zohar
"The Holy One, blessed be He, wants the heart."
So too we say "And a shekel I will bring,"
through the yearning and the will
"With righteousness he uttered the account of Ki Sisa" —
in the manner of the verse,
"And let our lips take the place of the bulls" (Hoshea 14:3):
that the reading of the parshah be considered
just as we read in Mussaf
"The light of Your countenance upon us, exalted Lord" —
that the sin of the Calf be rectified
and there be returned to us

paragraphs.text: Piyyut for Mussaf of Parshas Shekalim, “Eshkol ivvuy,” refrain — “Master, lift the light of Your face upon us. I shall bear a shekel in a house established and exalted. In righteousness, utter the assessment of ‘When you take a census.’ Shield us with protection, God, high and exalted.” The refrain returns before the conclusions of the seven blessings, with its final petition adapted to each blessing. These are the three recurring lines developed throughout this discourse.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Purim Katan 1 — “Sefer Urim V'Tumim already wrote that we may interpret the wording of the Shulchan Aruch even if they did not intend it, for the true matter is included in their words, written with ruach hakodesh.” There Rav Tzadok applies the same principle to the Rema’s closing verse “v'tov lev mishteh tamid,” showing how an accepted text carries meanings beyond its author’s conscious intent.

paragraphs.text: Urim VeTumim, Kitzur Tokfo Kohen §§123–124, end — “In my view, there is no doubt that everything was set down in writing through Hashem’s guidance to them. Later authorities raised many difficulties against them and resolved them with sharp and deep reasoning. Likewise, they included many laws in the sweetness and brevity of their wording. Surely they did not intend all of them, for how would this have been possible given the great labor, the heavenly labor, incumbent upon them? Who could compose a work on the entire Torah, drawn from all the earlier and later authorities, without the labor, the heavenly labor, weighing heavily upon him? Rather, the spirit of Hashem stirred within them so that their language would accord with the halachah without the writer’s conscious intention, and Hashem’s purpose prospered in their hands.” Eybeschütz is discussing the accepted authority of the Shulchan Aruch and Rema. Rav Tzadok extends this reasoning to accepted liturgical poems.

paragraphs.text: Zohar III 293a, Idra Zuta 31:1,3 — “This forehead is red as a rose. When the forehead of Atika is revealed in this forehead, it turns white as snow; that hour is called a time of goodwill for all. ... On Shabbat, at the time of the Mincha prayer, so that judgments should not awaken, the Holy Ancient One reveals His forehead. All judgments are subdued and quieted, and are not carried out.” The revelation is placed explicitly at Shabbat Mincha. Rav Tzadok relates the third meal to that revelation and reads the piyyut’s light of the face through it.

paragraphs.text: Shabbat 151b — “‘Before the sun and the light grow dark’ — these are the forehead and the nose; ‘and the moon’ — this is the soul; ‘and the stars’ — these are the cheeks.” The Gemara reads the verse as a description of human aging. Rav Tzadok draws on its association between light and the countenance when interpreting the piyut.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Pri Tzaddik, Vayechi 10 — “At the meal of Atika we ask for the revelation of the light… even though Atika is the intellect hidden from every thought, and of it is said ‘He made darkness His hiding place.’” Rav Tzadok there resolves the same tension present here: we petition for the light of Atika upon us precisely because it is beyond all grasp.

paragraphs.text: Shabbat 88b — “The congregation of Israel said before the Holy One, blessed be He: ‘Master of the world, even though my Beloved constricts and embitters my lot, He lodges between my breasts.’ ‘A cluster of henna is my beloved to me in the vineyards of Ein Gedi’ — He to Whom everything belongs atones for the sin of the kid that I gathered to myself.” The exposition joins eshkol with “He to Whom all belongs,” kofer with atonement, and gedi with the Calf. Rav Tzadok builds his reading of the piyut on these word associations.

paragraphs.text: Berakhot 11b — “But then, concerning ‘Who makes peace and creates evil,’ do we say it as it is written? Rather, it is written ‘evil,’ but we say ‘everything,’ using a more refined expression.” The Gemara explains the wording of the blessing preceding Shema. Rav Tzadok treats “everything” as including what is described in the verse as evil, rather than as excluding it.

paragraphs.text: Maggid of Mezritch, Ohr Torah (Remazei Torah), Bereishis §7, “Yesh litmoah” — “One must wonder at what is written in the Torah, ‘Behold, very good,’ several times in the work of creation, whereas in Deuteronomy it is written, ‘See, I have set before you today life and good, death and evil.’ Where did evil come from? The meaning, however, is not actual evil as we speak of it. Rather, evil too is good, but it is a lower degree than complete goodness. ... When people act well, evil too becomes good; when they sin, Heaven forbid, it becomes actual evil. For example, a broom is made to clear the house: it is somewhat good, though of a lower degree. But when one must strike a child with it after he sins, the broom becomes wholly evil, and they strike the child with it.” The opening asks about Deuteronomy 30:15. Rav Tzadok restates the question through Isaiah 45:7. The digital edition notes that “very good” actually occurs once, qualifying the opening’s “several times.”

paragraphs.text: Shabbat 149b — “‘Even punishing the righteous is not good’: ‘not good’ means evil, as it is written, ‘For You are not a God Who desires wickedness; evil shall not dwell with You.’ You are righteous, Hashem, and evil shall not dwell in Your dwelling.” Rav Tzadok uses the Gemara’s identification of “not good” with evil in interpreting the absence of “that it was good” in particular stages of creation.

paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Vayeshev 4 — “Come and see: When the Holy One, blessed be He, created the world, He created the angel of death from the first day. From where is this known? Rabbi Berechyah said: Because it is written, ‘Darkness was upon the face of the deep’ — this is the angel of death, who darkens the faces of creatures.” This identifies the darkness mentioned at creation with mortality, the particular form of darkness invoked here.

paragraphs.text: Bava Batra 16a — “Reish Lakish said: He is Satan, he is the evil inclination, and he is the Angel of Death. He is Satan, as it is written, ‘Satan went out from before Hashem.’ He is the evil inclination: there it is written, ‘Only evil all day,’ and here it is written, ‘Only do not stretch out your hand against him.’ He is the Angel of Death, as it is written, ‘Only preserve his life’—showing that it is in his power.”

paragraphs.text: Pesachim 54a — “Rabbi Yosei says: The fire that the Holy One, blessed be He, created on the second day has no extinction forever. Rabbi Benaah son of Rabbi Ulla said: Why was ‘that it was good’ not said on the second day? Because the fire of Gehinnom was created on it. Rabbi Elazar said: Although ‘that it was good’ was not said on it, Scripture returned and included it on the sixth day, saying, ‘God saw everything that He had made, and behold, it was very good.’” The source explicitly joins the second day’s omission to the comprehensive judgment of the sixth day; it supplies the structure of Rav Tzadok’s argument here.

paragraphs.text: Zohar, Tetzaveh 10 — “Words of Torah become settled only there. There is no light except that which emerges from darkness: when this side is subdued, the Holy One, blessed be He, is raised on high and honored in His glory. There is no service of the Holy One, blessed be He, except from within darkness, and no good except from within evil. When a person enters an evil path and then abandons it, the Holy One, blessed be He, is exalted in His glory. The completion of everything therefore lies in good and evil together, and afterward in ascending through the good; there is no good except that which has emerged from evil. Through this good His glory is exalted, and this is complete service.” The passage describes leaving the evil path, not remaining in it. It clarifies how transformed darkness becomes the occasion for a fuller revelation of divine glory. The source is identified by its preserved section coordinate; the manuscript’s traditional folio awaits separate collation.

paragraphs.text: Bereshit Rabbah 9:7,9–10 — “‘Behold, very good’—this is the good inclination; ‘and behold, very good’—this is the evil inclination. Is the evil inclination very good? Without the evil inclination a person would not build a house, marry, beget children, or engage in business. ... Rabbi Zeira said: ‘Behold, very good’—this is the Garden of Eden; ‘and behold, very good’—this is Gehinnom. ... Whoever accumulates commandments and good deeds—there is the Garden of Eden; whoever does not—there is Gehinnom. Rabbi Shmuel bar Yitzchak said: ‘Behold, very good’—this is the angel of life; ‘and behold, very good’—this is the angel of death. ... Whoever accumulates commandments and good deeds—there is the angel of life; whoever does not—there is the angel of death.” These are separate expositions within the same section. They distinguish the role of human conduct while identifying a purpose for forces commonly experienced as evil.

paragraphs.text: Shabbat 89b — “Rabbi Yitzchak said: The Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel: If your sins are like these years that have been arranged and have come from the six days of creation until now, they shall become white as snow.” The Gemara expounds shanim as years rather than merely as scarlet. Rav Tzadok relates this wording to the divine ordering of history and to the transformation accomplished by repentance.

paragraphs.text: Rashi on Rosh Hashanah 30a — “If you ask how it could be built on the fifteenth, on the festival, or built at night, when we maintain that the Temple is built neither on a festival nor at night: That applies to a building made by human hands; but the building of the future will be by the hands of Heaven.” Rashi offers this distinction in explaining Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai’s concern that the Temple might appear too late for the omer offering to be prepared by midday.

paragraphs.text: Zevachim 46b — “‘A pleasing aroma’ — for the sake of bringing satisfaction. ‘To Hashem’ — for the sake of Him Who spoke and the world came into being.” The Gemara enumerates the intended purposes of an offering. Rashi explains the satisfaction as that His will was expressed and fulfilled; Rav Tzadok emphasizes the desire to carry out that will.

paragraphs.text: Zohar III 160a, Shlach 10:7 — “What do those children of faith say? ‘If Hashem desires us, He will give it to us.’ Once a person strives toward the Holy One, blessed be He, with the desire of the heart, He asks of us only the heart, and that they guard that holy mark, as it is written, ‘Your people are all righteous; they shall inherit the land forever.’” The source joins inward desire with guarding the holy mark of the covenant. Rav Tzadok applies the value of that desire to a commandment whose outward performance is presently unavailable.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 106b — “Rav Yehudah would remove his shoes and rain would come, whereas we cry out and no attention is paid to us. Rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, desires the heart, as it is written: ‘Hashem sees into the heart.’” The contrast concerns the efficacy of prayer despite later scholars’ extensive learning. Rav Tzadok invokes it for the value of sincere desire when the sacrificial action is unavailable.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Menachos 110a — “Whoever engages in the Torah of the chatas is as if he offered a chatas, and whoever engages in the Torah of the asham is as if he offered an asham.” The Gemara supplies the principle that reading the parsha of an offering stands in place of the deed, so that the reading of Parshas Shekalim itself counts as giving the shekalim.
